title: What training supports Modern Slavery Act reporting?
description: How staff training supports reporting under the Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth): the mandatory criteria, who must report, and where reform stands in 2026.
shortAnswer: The Modern Slavery Act 2018 (Cth) does not mandate training, but it requires entities with annual consolidated revenue of at least $100 million to describe the actions they take to assess and address modern slavery risks, and how they assess the effectiveness of those actions. The Act itself gives staff training as an example of such an action, so training is one of the most commonly reported and scrutinised measures.
keyTakeaways: Reporting entities must give an annual modern slavery statement within 6 months after the end of their reporting period, addressing the mandatory criteria in section 16.
Section 16(1)(d) requires a description of actions to assess and address risks; the Act's own example includes providing training for staff about modern slavery.
Section 16(1)(e) requires a description of how the entity assesses the effectiveness of its actions, which completion counts alone do not show.
The government's December 2024 response to the statutory review agreed to 25 of 30 recommendations, including options such as penalties and due diligence; as at September 2026 these are not yet law.
Procurement, supplier management and HR staff are the priority audiences, because they control the operations and supply chain risks the statement describes.
regulator: Attorney-General's Department (administers the Act); Australian Anti-Slavery Commissioner (promotes compliance)
appliesTo: Entities based or operating in Australia with annual consolidated revenue of at least $100 million
The Commonwealth, on behalf of non-corporate Commonwealth entities

sections.heading: Who must report under the Modern Slavery Act?

blocks.text: Entities based or operating in the Australian market with annual consolidated revenue of at least $100 million must report. The [Attorney-General's Department (AGD)](https://www.ag.gov.au/crime/people-smuggling-and-human-trafficking/modern-slavery) describes the Act, in force since January 1, 2019, as establishing a national reporting requirement for large businesses and other entities, with statements published on the [Modern Slavery Statements Register](https://modernslaveryregister.gov.au/).

The Commonwealth reports on behalf of non-corporate Commonwealth entities through an annual Commonwealth Modern Slavery Statement. Other entities may report voluntarily. Under section 13 of the [Modern Slavery Act 2018](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2018A00153/latest/versions), a statement for a single reporting entity must be given to the Minister within 6 months after the end of the entity's reporting period and approved by its principal governing body.

sections.heading: What do the mandatory criteria say, and where does training fit?

blocks.text: Section 16 sets seven mandatory criteria, and training evidence is most relevant to two of them: actions taken (paragraph (d)) and effectiveness (paragraph (e)). The Act's example for paragraph (d) states that actions "may include the development of policies and processes to address modern slavery risks, and providing training for staff about modern slavery".

sections.heading: Who should receive modern slavery training?

blocks.text: Prioritize the people whose decisions shape the risks the statement describes: procurement and category managers, supplier relationship owners, HR and recruitment teams, and the executives and board who approve the statement. General awareness for all staff is useful, but targeted role training produces the evidence that paragraphs (d) and (e) require.

sections.heading: How do you show training is effective for section 16(1)(e)?

blocks.text: Report outcomes, not only inputs. A statement that says a percentage of procurement staff completed a module describes an action; it does not describe how the entity assesses whether that action is working.

items: Assessment scores on role scenarios, compared year on year.
The share of high-risk supplier onboardings with completed due diligence, before and after training.
Number and quality of escalations raised by trained staff.
Findings from supplier audits or grievance mechanisms that trained staff acted on.
Board briefing records showing the approving body understood what it signed.

blocks.text: These measures connect to the method in [how to evidence training effectiveness to a regulator](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator).

sections.heading: What reforms are coming, and what has changed already?

blocks.text: As at September 2026, the reporting criteria are unchanged, but reform is in development. The Act's only amendments since 2018 took effect in 2024, including the establishment of the Australian Anti-Slavery Commissioner, whose statutory functions include promoting compliance with the Act.

items: May 25, 2023: the report of the statutory review led by Professor John McMillan AO was tabled, making 30 recommendations, including penalties for non-compliance, lowering the threshold from $100 million to $50 million, and requiring a due diligence system.
December 2, 2024: the government response agreed, in full, in part or in principle, to 25 of the 30 recommendations and noted 5.

July 21, 2025 to September 1, 2025: AGD's public consultation on strengthening the Act, followed by workshops to April 2026 covering reporting criteria, compliance and enforcement, due diligence, and a power to declare high-risk matters.
August 3, 2026: AGD reported consulting 630 stakeholders across 24 workshops and receiving over 200 submissions, which are informing ongoing development of reforms.

blocks.title: What this means for training owners
blocks.text: If a due diligence obligation or penalties are legislated, training records will move from supporting evidence to proof of compliance. Building role-based training with assessment now, and recording which risk each module addresses, prepares for that change without teaching draft proposals as current law. The timeline is drawn from AGD's [consultation page](https://consultations.ag.gov.au/crime/modern-slavery-act/).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each section 16 criterion to the concepts, audiences and assessment points that support it, so the evidence for a modern slavery statement comes from one structured record. When the Act is amended, the affected criteria can be traced to the training that depends on them.

faqs.q: Is modern slavery training mandatory in Australia?
faqs.a: Not under the current Act. The Modern Slavery Act 2018 requires reporting entities to describe their actions, and gives staff training as an example of an action. An entity that reports no training will have less to say under section 16(1)(d) and (e), which is why most statements describe training.

faqs.q: What happens if a reporting entity does not comply?
faqs.a: Under section 16A, the Minister may request an explanation or remedial action within at least 28 days, and may publish information about an entity that fails to comply with that request. As at September 2026 the Act has no financial penalties, although the statutory review recommended introducing them.

No. As at September 2026 the threshold remains annual consolidated revenue of at least $100 million. The statutory review recommended lowering it to $50 million, and the government has consulted on implementing review recommendations, but no amending legislation has been passed.

The Act does not require it, but section 16 asks for actions across operations and supply chains. Many reporting entities share awareness material with high-risk suppliers or include training expectations in supplier codes, and report this as an action under section 16(1)(d).
